title: Why We Should Still Learn Languages After 60
paragraphs: Many people believe that it is too late to learn a new language once they reach old age. However, a growing body of research suggests that learning a language later in life may still benefit the brain.

In July 2026, researchers presented a study at the Federation of European Neuroscience Societies Forum, a major neuroscience conference. The study involved hundreds of people in Spain's Basque region who spoke between one and four languages, including Spanish, Basque, French and English. Using artificial intelligence, the researchers estimated each person's "brain age" based on patterns of connections in their brains.

The results were striking. The brains of people who spoke two languages appeared to be about six years younger than those of people who spoke only one. For people who spoke three languages, the difference was about seven years, and for those who spoke four, it was roughly 13 years. People who had learned a second language earlier in life and become very fluent seemed to benefit the most.

However, according to neuroscientist Tommy Wood, who was not involved in the study, there is no clear age at which learning a language stops being beneficial. Wood pointed out that several randomized controlled trials involving older adults have found improvements in attention, working memory and other thinking skills after just a few months of language learning. For example, a 2024 study of 41 adults aged 60 to 80 found that their performance on a test of attention improved after a language-learning program.
Learning a language can also encourage people to stay socially active. Wood also advised learners not to be afraid of making mistakes, which he described as one of the biggest drivers of learning.

Nevertheless, the evidence is not entirely consistent. For example, one study in China found that while older adults improved their thinking skills after a six-month language course, people who played games such as sudoku and crossword puzzles improved just as much. In addition, two studies in 2023 found almost no difference in thinking skills after language-learning programs.
Still, research shows that older adults can be very successful language learners, so age should not be a reason to give up.
